body:
Bronze sculpture as a continuing tradition

The use of metal casting in India has a long history extending back to the Harappan Civilisation. Over time, craftsmen developed the ability to produce increasingly elaborate images in copper alloys.

Bronze sculpture differs from stone relief because a cast image can be produced as a separate, three-dimensional object. Many metal images were used in temples, monasteries and religious ceremonies, while metalworking also served everyday needs.

The lost-wax technique, known as cire-perdue, remained particularly important. A wax model was enclosed within a mould, the wax was removed through heating and molten metal was introduced to reproduce the form.

Early and Gupta-period bronze traditions

Metal figures from the Harappan period demonstrate that the essential casting technology was known in the 3rd millennium BCE.

Later bronze traditions developed in several regions. Gupta and post-Gupta Buddha images from northern India frequently show refined body proportions and carefully represented monastic robes.

Bronze images influenced by the Mathura style may display prominent garment folds. Images influenced by the Sarnath style often show much less visible drapery.

Chola bronze sculpture

The Chola dynasty of Tamil Nadu patronised an exceptionally refined tradition of bronze sculpture, particularly from the 10th to the 12th centuries CE.

Chola bronzes are known for balanced proportions, carefully modelled bodies, flowing poses and clear religious attributes.

Several images were designed for ritual use. Their portability distinguished them from sculptures permanently attached to temple walls.

Shiva as Nataraja

The Nataraja image represents Shiva in a dancing form. It became one of the most recognisable achievements of Chola bronze sculpture.

A typical Nataraja image includes:

  • Upper right hand: Holds a damaru, a small drum.
  • Upper left hand: Holds fire.
  • Lower right hand: Displays abhaya mudra, the gesture of reassurance.
  • Lower left hand: Extends across the body and directs attention towards the raised foot.
  • Raised leg: Contributes to the characteristic dynamic dancing posture.
  • Supporting foot: Presses upon Apasmara, the figure associated with ignorance.
  • Surrounding arch: A ring of flames frames the dancing form.

The composition unites movement and balance. The image's religious symbolism is expressed through recognisable attributes and bodily position.

Other Chola bronze forms

Chola sculptors produced images of several Hindu figures, including Parvati and different forms of Shiva and Vishnu.

Sembiyan Mahadevi, a Chola queen of the 10th century CE, was an important patron of religious art.

The tradition also includes representations such as Ardhanarishvara, combining masculine and feminine aspects of Shiva and Parvati within a single figure.

Pala-period bronze sculpture

In eastern India, especially Bihar and Bengal, bronze casting developed under the Palas.

Nalanda and Kurkihar were important centres associated with Buddhist metal images. Subjects included the Buddha, Bodhisattvas and figures associated with Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhist traditions.

Images of Avalokiteshvara and Tara became important within this artistic tradition.

Many Pala-period images show delicate ornamentation and clear iconographic details while retaining influences from earlier Gupta sculpture.

Jain bronze sculpture

Jain communities also patronised metal images of Tirthankaras. Early examples include bronzes from Chausa in Bihar, associated with the Kushana period.

The Akota bronze hoard near Vadodara, Gujarat, provides important evidence of early medieval Jain metal sculpture in western India.

Among the figures represented in Jain bronze traditions are Adinatha or Rishabhanatha, Parshvanatha and Mahavira. Adinatha may be recognised by long hairlocks, while Parshvanatha is frequently represented with a serpent canopy.

Stone and bronze compared

Stone sculpture is shaped principally by removing material through carving. Bronze sculpture is generally produced by introducing molten metal into a prepared mould.

Stone reliefs usually remain part of their original architectural surface. Bronze images can be made separately and moved, although some are permanently installed.

Both traditions required specialised knowledge and could represent similar religious subjects. Their differences lie chiefly in material, production and the possibilities offered by each medium.

Prelims focus

  • Chola bronze sculpture flourished especially during the 10th–12th centuries CE.
  • Nataraja is a major Chola bronze form representing Shiva in a dancing posture.
  • Nataraja's upper right hand holds a damaru; the upper left holds fire.
  • Apasmara represents ignorance beneath the dancing figure.
  • Nalanda and Kurkihar are important eastern Indian centres of Buddhist bronze sculpture.
  • Trap: Akota is associated with Jain bronzes in Gujarat, not Chola bronzes from Tamil Nadu.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 7, 'Indian Bronze Sculpture', printed pp. 103–108, and Chapter 6, printed pp. 92–95.]

body:
Gujarat's place in Indian sculpture

Gujarat preserves important artistic remains from the Harappan period through the early historic and medieval periods. Its heritage includes terracotta and metal objects, Buddhist stone sculpture, Jain bronzes and elaborately carved temples and stepwells.

The state's sculptural history is therefore not associated with a single dynasty or religious tradition. Different materials and styles developed in different historical settings.

Harappan artistic centres in Gujarat

Lothal and Dholavira demonstrate Gujarat's role within the Harappan Civilisation of approximately 2600–1900 BCE.

At Lothal, bead production and metalworking provide evidence of specialised crafts. Finds include copper animal figures, while the broader Harappan tradition includes seals, pottery and terracotta objects.

Dholavira is particularly significant for stone construction and urban remains. These sites show how artistic and technical skills formed part of everyday and commercial life.

Devni Mori: Early Buddhist remains

Devni Mori, near Shamlaji in the Aravalli region of Gujarat, preserves evidence of an early Buddhist establishment. The remains include a stupa and monastery associated with approximately the 3rd–4th centuries CE.

Excavation of the stupa revealed an inscribed relic casket. Its inscription identifies the contents as bodily relics of the Buddha.

Devni Mori is important because it connects the wider Buddhist stupa tradition with archaeological evidence from Gujarat.

Khambhalida: Buddhist rock-cut sculpture

The Khambhalida Caves, near Gondal in Rajkot district, belong approximately to the 4th–5th centuries CE.

The central cave contains a stupa and is associated with the chaitya tradition. Its entrance is flanked by sculpted Bodhisattva figures identified as Padmapani and Vajrapani.

The caves were excavated in local limestone. Their sculptures demonstrate the presence of Buddhist image-making traditions in western India.

Shamlaji and early medieval stone sculpture

Shamlaji in Gujarat is associated with important sculptural remains dating approximately from the 6th–8th centuries CE.

Several sculptures from the region were made in grey schist. They show an interaction between local artistic traditions and wider post-Gupta sculptural developments.

Shamlaji therefore helps explain how the influence of Gupta artistic forms could be adapted to regional materials and preferences.

Akota and Jain bronze images

Akota, near present-day Vadodara, is known for a significant hoard of Jain bronze images dating to the early medieval period.

These works represent Tirthankaras and associated figures. They demonstrate the continuing use of sophisticated metal casting in western India after the Gupta period.

Akota is particularly important when comparing regional bronze traditions: Gujarat's early medieval Jain images are distinct from the later Chola bronzes of Tamil Nadu.

Modhera: Solanki-period stone carving

The Sun Temple at Modhera in Gujarat belongs to the early 11th century CE and is associated with the Solanki or Chaulukya dynasty, particularly Bhima I.

The temple is noted for elaborate stone sculpture, ornamented architectural elements and its relationship with a large stepped tank known as the Surya Kund.

The tank contains 108 miniature shrines arranged among the steps. The temple's decorative programme illustrates the integration of sculpture with architecture and water-related sacred space.

Rani ki Vav: Sculptural decoration in a stepwell

Rani ki Vav at Patan, Gujarat, is an outstanding example of the Maru-Gurjara style of architecture and sculpture.

Constructed in the 11th century CE, the stepwell was originally conceived as a memorial to a king. It combines a practical water-storage structure with elaborate religious, mythological and other sculptural representations.

The monument is designed as an inverted temple celebrating the importance of water. It has 7 levels of stairs and sculptural panels.

Its decorative programme includes more than 500 principal sculptures and over 1000 smaller figures. Vishnu and related religious themes are prominent, alongside other subjects.

Rani ki Vav was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2014 under cultural criteria (i) and (iv). This inscription status is recorded as of 23 November 2026.

Matching Gujarat sites with their identifying features

SiteLocationPrincipal association
LothalGujaratHarappan crafts, beads and metal objects

KhambhalidaRajkot districtBuddhist rock-cut caves and Bodhisattva sculptures
ShamlajiAravalli regionEarly medieval grey-schist sculpture
AkotaNear VadodaraEarly medieval Jain bronze hoard
ModheraGujaratSolanki-period Sun Temple and sculpted Surya Kund
Rani ki VavPatan11th-century Maru-Gurjara stepwell sculpture

One-glance chronology of Indian sculpture

The main developments can be arranged in a broad historical sequence. Prehistoric painting precedes Harappan urban art; Mauryan monumental stone sculpture is followed by more elaborate Buddhist stupa reliefs; the Kushana and Gupta periods establish influential forms of the Buddha image; and medieval regional traditions produce monumental temple reliefs and sophisticated bronze icons.

The sequence is a guide to principal developments, not a claim that one style disappeared when another emerged. Stone carving, terracotta production and metal casting often continued simultaneously.

Important distinctions across the whole topic

  • Bhimbetka and Lakhudiyar: Prehistoric rock paintings rather than temple sculpture.
  • Harappan art: Small stone, terracotta and metal objects alongside seals and craft products.
  • Mauryan art: Polished pillars, animal capitals and monumental figures.
  • Bharhut, Sanchi and Amaravati: Buddhist stupa reliefs with distinct regional treatments.
  • Gandhara and Mathura: Major early centres of human Buddha images.
  • Gupta Sarnath: Refined Buddha forms with transparent-looking drapery.
  • Medieval schools: Regional stone sculpture and elaborate temple carving.
  • Chola tradition: Refined bronze images, especially Nataraja.

Prelims focus

  • Devni Mori: Buddhist stupa and inscribed relic casket near Shamlaji.
  • Khambhalida: Buddhist caves with Padmapani and Vajrapani sculptures in Rajkot district.
  • Akota: Jain bronze images near Vadodara.
  • Modhera: Solanki-period Sun Temple, associated with Bhima I.
  • Rani ki Vav: Patan; 11th century CE; UNESCO World Heritage inscription in 2014.
  • Trap: The UNESCO-listed Bhimbetka rock shelters are in Madhya Pradesh; Rani ki Vav is in Gujarat.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class XI, Chapter 2, printed pp. 9–17; Chapter 4, printed pp. 31–33; Chapter 6, printed pp. 75–76 and 94–95; Chapter 7, printed pp. 103–106; Gujarat Tourism, 'Dev Ni Mori', Aravalli, consulted 23 November 2026; Gujarat Tourism, Rangilo Rajkot, section 'Khambhalida Caves', consulted 23 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Rani-ki-Vav (the Queen's Stepwell) at Patan, Gujarat', World Heritage List no. 922, inscription 2014, consulted 23 November 2026.]
